sights.w: The 1917 Beaux-Arts capitol at the heart of the Isthmus — the only granite capitol dome in the US. Free tours cover the rotunda mural 'The Resources of Wisconsin', and the summer observation deck gives a 360° view of the lakes. A National Historic Landmark (2001).
sights.k: free tours; observation deck in summer

sights.w: Frank Lloyd Wright's 1938 design for a civic center on Lake Monona, rejected by one vote and built only in 1997, nearly four decades after his death. The free rooftop garden is the city's best lake-and-Capitol view.

The lakeside terrace of the 1928 Memorial Union on Lake Mendota — the city's 'unofficial living room', with sunburst chairs in John Deere green, Allis-Chalmers orange and yellow, a beer and a Babcock cone at sunset. The Union is on the National Register.
16 acres of free outdoor gardens on Lake Monona plus the Bolz Conservatory glass pyramid — and the gilded Royal Thai Pavilion, a gift of the Thai government and the only one on the US mainland.

The world's first restored ecological communities — prairies, savannas and wetlands started by Aldo Leopold and CCC crews in the 1930s — now a National Historic Landmark (2021) with a free trail network. Atlas Obscura's 'Lost City Forest' is the failed 1920s subdivision inside it.

sights.address: 5607 County Rd C, Spring Green, WI 53588
sights.w: Frank Lloyd Wright's home, studio and 600-acre estate in the Wyoming Valley, the exemplar of the Prairie School — a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2019 (the 20th-Century Architecture of Frank Lloyd Wright). Tours from the visitor center.

Alex Jordan Jr.'s maximalist fever-dream (1945–59) atop a rock chimney near Spring Green — the cantilevered Infinity Room, automaton music machines and the world's largest indoor carousel. Time Out calls it a must from Madison; it sits minutes from Taliesin.

sights.address: Devil's Lake State Park, south of Baraboo, Sauk County, WI
sights.w: Wisconsin's largest state park (1911), a glacial lake ringed by 500-foot pink-quartzite bluffs in the Baraboo Range, 35 miles from Madison — the Devil's Doorway trail is the classic short climb.

A limestone show cave in the south slope of the East Blue Mound, discovered by quarrymen in 1939 — a National Natural Landmark (1987) that the Chicago Academy of Sciences called 'the significant cave of the upper Midwest'.
Barry Levenson's free museum of 7,000+ mustards (and mustard memorabilia) in downtown Middleton, with a tasting bar — Wisconsin roadside whimsy at its best.
A 28-acre AZA-accredited county zoo beside Lake Wingra that has been free since 1904 — a condition of the Vilas family's land gift.
